c.tagline: Sugar-town-turned-resort gateway to Saona, golf, and a Mediterranean village.

taxi.fareNote: Uber operates but coverage is limited outside the resorts; most taxis are unmetered, so agree the fare before you get in. Motoconcho scooter-taxis are the cheapest way around town.

emergency.note: 911 is the national emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance across the Dominican Republic.

avoid.reason: No formal no-go zones, but skip the low-income barrios away from the Marina, Casa de Campo and central tourist areas after dark due to street crime.
Motorbike bag-snatching and pickpocketing occur downtown and around the public market; keep phones out of sight.

hood_desc: The working heart of the city around the Parque Central and Mercado Modelo, with local eateries, shops, and the cruise port; the most authentic, walkable base and the cheapest place to stay.

A private, gated 7,000-acre resort community next to the city with three championship golf courses (Teeth of the Dog is rated the Caribbean's best), a marina, equestrian center, private beaches, and the Altos de Chavón artisan village; best for a self-contained luxury stay.
The stylish yacht harbor within Casa de Campo, designed to feel like an Italian fishing village, lined with waterfront restaurants, designer boutiques, and bars; the area's dining-and-nightlife hub.

A laid-back fishing village east of the city and the launch point for boats to Isla Saona and Isla Catalina and the gateway to Parque Nacional del Este; a mix of local color, dive shops, and small hotels.
The beach-resort strip just south of Bayahíbe fronting the long white-sand Playa Dominicus, packed with all-inclusive resorts; a relaxed, family-friendly base for sun and diving.

water.note: Drink bottled water; tap water is not considered safe for visitors.

transit.hours: Guaguas and city públicos run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM; motoconchos and taxis fill late-night gaps.
transit.note: La Romana has no metro, tram, or rail; getting around means shared guaguas/públicos (minivans and cars on fixed routes), motoconcho scooter-taxis, and regular taxis.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver (públicos around 20-30 pesos, motoconchos a bit more); there is no rechargeable transit card.

bus: Express coaches to Santo Domingo, Higüey & Punta Cana (Expreso Bávaro, SITRABAPU)
ferry: Cruise terminal at Casa de Campo
Day-trip boats from Bayahíbe to Isla Saona & Isla Catalina

transit.m: Taxi to La Romana / Casa de Campo (10-15 min)
Guagua/públicos from the main road into town (cash, ~20 min)

tip.r: Restaurants add a 10% 'ley' service charge plus 18% tax; leaving another 5-10% for good service is customary.

landmarks: Altos de Chavón
A remarkable recreation of a 16th-century Mediterranean village built in stone above the Chavón River, complete with artisan studios, church and museum.
Altos de Chavón Amphitheater
A 5,000-seat Grecian-style stone amphitheater inaugurated by Frank Sinatra in 1982, still hosting concerts under Caribbean stars above the river gorge.
Río Chavón
A jungle-walled river winding beneath Altos de Chavón, so cinematic it starred in Apocalypse Now and Rambo; boat cruises drift its glassy waters.
Casa de Campo Marina
A glamorous Portofino-styled marina of megayachts, boutiques and waterfront restaurants at the heart of the Caribbean's most famous resort community.
Regional Museum of Archaeology (Altos de Chavón)
An excellent small museum holding one of the country's best collections of pre-Columbian Taíno artifacts, from ceremonial axes to shamanic figures.
Parque Central and Iglesia Santa Rosa de Lima
The city's true center, where the modest 20th-century church of La Romana's patron saint overlooks an obelisk-adorned plaza and everyday Dominican life.
Teeth of the Dog Golf Course
Pete Dye's 1971 seaside masterpiece at Casa de Campo, a par-72 course with seven ocean-hugging holes carved from coral coastline, ranked among the world's best.
Dye Fore Golf Course
A 27-hole Pete Dye course perched on cliffs above the Chavón River canyon, with fairways overlooking the marina, the Caribbean Sea and Altos de Chavón.
Central Romana Sugar Mill
The vast sugar mill built in 1917 that gave rise to La Romana as a company town, once the world's largest single-mill cane harvester.
Playa Minitas
A sheltered white-sand beach within Casa de Campo, with calm turquoise water and palm trees framing one of the resort's most popular stretches of shore.

train.note: The Dominican Republic has no intercity passenger railway. The track that still exists around La Romana belongs to Central Romana Corporation and is a private sugar-cane system - it hauls cane to the mill and only very occasionally runs an excursion train, not a scheduled service. The country's only public rail is the Santo Domingo Metro run by OPRET (https://www.opret.gob.do/), about two hours west, and there is nothing crossing the border to Haiti. Coaches and cars are the only ground transport.

bus.note: Guaguas and express coaches (Expreso Bávaro, SITRABAPU) run to Santo Domingo (~2 hr), Higüey, and Punta Cana; there are no international bus services.

ferry.note: La Romana's port is a cruise-ship terminal at Casa de Campo; passenger boats from nearby Bayahíbe serve Isla Saona and Isla Catalina as day trips rather than scheduled transport.

half.name: Bayahíbe
half.blurb: A picturesque fishing village and dive hub, gateway to Parque Nacional del Este and the boats to Saona and Catalina.

half.name: Cueva de las Maravillas
half.blurb: A lit show-cave between La Romana and San Pedro with pre-Columbian Taíno pictographs and petroglyphs.

half.name: Bayahibe
half.blurb: A once-sleepy fishing village east of La Romana, now the launch point for Saona trips, with a pretty beach and excellent scuba diving.

full.name: Isla Saona
full.blurb: A postcard Caribbean island inside Parque Nacional del Este with white sand, natural starfish pools, and calm turquoise water.

full.name: Isla Catalina
full.blurb: A small offshore island famous for the 'Wall' and 'Aquarium' dive sites and clear snorkeling reefs.

full.name: Santo Domingo
full.blurb: The capital's Zona Colonial, the oldest European city in the Americas, about two hours west.
